outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no accepted resolution of the abc conjecture has appeared. Mochizuki's 2012 IUT claim remains contested; Kirti Joshi's 2024 to 2026 arXiv papers claim to complete it but are unrefereed and disputed; the ZEN University LANA interim report (17 July 2026) withholds judgement and localises the same Corollary 3.12 step that Scholze and Stix flagged in 2018. The window also holds bounds on the count of exceptional triples (Browning, Lichtman, Teräväinen 2024 with a 2026 revision; Lichtman 2025; Bernert 2025; Li 2025), which move the count but not finiteness, a single-author 2026 note (Carella) claiming infinitely many exceptional triples for small ε (which would contradict the conjecture; unrefereed), and results conditional on abc (AxiomProver, 2026).
problem_asks: (1) For every real ε > 0: a universal claim over ε. (2) For each such ε, the set of positive integer triples (a, b, c) with a + b = c and rad(abc)^(1+ε) < c is finite, where rad(n) is the product of the distinct primes dividing n. The bullet asks for finiteness only: no effective bound, no constant, and no claim for any particular ε. Read literally, the bullet does not require gcd(a, b, c) = 1. Without coprimality the statement is false: (a, b, c) = (2^n, 2^n, 2^(n+1)) has rad(abc) = 2 and c = 2^(n+1) > 2^(1+ε) for all large n, giving infinitely many triples for every ε > 0. Every source in this record, including Wikipedia’s own statement, uses the coprime reading, and this record does too; the difference is flagged for the judging pass. The parent n-conjecture is not asked here: this bullet is the three-integer case.

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, ‘Note on the ABC Conjecture’ (arXiv math/0606221, submitted 9 June 2006). The abstract says it offers heuristic arguments and theoretical evidence that contradict the abc conjecture over the rationals. Discussion only: no proof and no partial result. Pre-window; recorded because the same author posted the 2026 note in event carella-2026-note.
events.delivers: Heuristic evidence against the abc conjecture. No theorem.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; nothing established.
events.doubts: Heuristic only. I read the abstract; the full text was not read.
events.direction: Argues heuristically against the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Shinichi Mochizuki (Kyoto, RIMS) posted four papers on inter-universal Teichmüller theory (IUT) in August 2012, claiming a proof of Szpiro’s conjecture and therefore of the abc conjecture (Wikipedia: ‘Since August 2012, Shinichi Mochizuki has claimed a proof of Szpiro's conjecture and therefore the abc conjecture’). The papers were later published in PRIMS, the RIMS journal Mochizuki edits; Mochizuki recused himself from the review. Wikipedia gives April 2020 for the announcement of publication (by two RIMS mathematicians) and March 2021 for publication. Per the first-public-argument rule the date is the 2012 posting, not the journal date.
events.revisions: Journal publication announced April 2020 and published March 2021 in PRIMS (Wikipedia). The 2012 date is kept per §5.1.
events.delivers: Claims the abc conjecture for every ε > 0, via IUT and Szpiro-type estimates (Wikipedia). I did not open the four 2012 papers.
events.remains: Nothing by the author’s own claim. The community has not accepted it: Wikipedia’s lead says the conjecture ‘is still regarded as unproven by the mainstream mathematical community’ and that the papers ‘have not been widely accepted’.

checked_by.qualification: Arithmetic geometers; spent a week at RIMS in March 2018 discussing the proof with Mochizuki and Hoshi
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote ‘Why abc is still a conjecture’ concluding there is no proof: a gap at the step from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 of the third IUT paper which small modifications will not rescue (as quoted by Wikipedia and secondary reports; the PDF was binary and unreadable to my tools)

checked_by.qualification: Editors at the institute that runs PRIMS; a special committee excluding Mochizuki reviewed the paper (per a search snippet, not opened)
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the papers for PRIMS; announced publication in April 2020

events.time_since_posted: not applicable: public engagement exists (see checked_by)
events.doubts: (a) Scholze and Stix’s 2018 gap at the Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 step; Mochizuki disputes it. (b) The journal is run by the author’s institute, and critics raised a conflict of interest (Earth.com, opened). (c) The 2026 LANA interim report says the Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 derivation is unclear to many members (see lana-2026-interim). (d) Kedlaya is reported (search snippet of a Nature article, not opened) to have said community opinion has not changed much since 2018.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture for every ε > 0, so it cuts for the conjecture.

events.what_happened: After a week of discussion at RIMS, Kyoto, in March 2018 with Mochizuki and Hoshi, Peter Scholze and Jakob Stix wrote ‘Why abc is still a conjecture’. They conclude there is no proof, and that the problem is structural: small modifications will not rescue the strategy. The gap is located at the step from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 of the third IUT paper, described by Stix as ‘serious, unfixable’ (secondary reports; PDF binary and unreadable to my tools).
events.revisions: Mochizuki posted it on his website with rebuttals (per a search snippet).
events.delivers: A critique. It argues that the IUT argument does not establish the abc inequality. It proves no result on abc.
events.remains: The whole problem, as far as the critique goes: it asserts no positive result.

checked_by.qualification: Arithmetic geometers who worked through the argument with its author in Kyoto
checked_by.what_they_did: Worked through the argument and reported a gap; concluded there is no proof

events.doubts: Mochizuki disputes the critique, attributing it to ‘certain fundamental misunderstandings’ (secondary report). Scholze later said ‘I believe the abc conjecture is still open’ (Quanta, per a search snippet).
events.direction: Cuts against the 2012 claim. It does not assert the conjecture is false.

events.what_happened: Abdelmajid Ben Hadj Salem, EasyChair preprint 2169 ‘Definitive Proof of The abc Conjecture’ (version 1 dated 16 December 2019). The abstract claims an elementary proof of c < rad²(abc), then a proof of abc for ε ≥ 1 and for ε in (0,1), with K(ε) = e^(1/ε²). I read the abstract and metadata only; the body was not read.
events.revisions: A version 2 is listed; its date is not shown.
events.delivers: Claims an unconditional proof of abc for all ε > 0 (per the abstract, which names no hypothesis). Body not checked.
events.remains: Nothing, by the claim.
events.doubts: EasyChair preprint; the page says it is not peer-reviewed. No engagement found. A separate 2025 conditional paper by the same author is reported in search (see incomplete).
events.direction: Claims the conjecture, so cuts for it.

events.what_happened: Kirti Joshi (University of Arizona), ‘Construction of Arithmetic Teichmüller Spaces III: A Rosetta Stone and a proof of Mochizuki’s Corollary 3.12’ (arXiv 2401.13508, v1 24 January 2024). The abstract claims a proof of Mochizuki’s Corollary 3.12, a ‘Rosetta Stone’ for reading IUT alongside Arithmetic Teichmüller Spaces, and the geometric case in §12. The abstract does not mention abc. On Woit’s blog (January 2024) Joshi was asked whether he claims abc; he replied that his conclusions would come in a later paper (Construction IV).
events.revisions: v2 15 March 2024; v3 27 June 2024; v4 24 February 2025 (current; the comments describe a substantially expanded version).
events.delivers: Claims a proof of Mochizuki’s Corollary 3.12, a step inside the IUT argument that Mochizuki uses to get abc. It does not claim abc in its abstract.
events.remains: The abc inequality itself. Whether the Corollary 3.12 result implies abc is exactly what Woit asked Joshi to state; not established in this paper’s abstract.

checked_by.qualification: Mathematical physicist at Columbia; blogs on the dispute
checked_by.what_they_did: Commented in January 2024 that expert uncertainty exists and asked Joshi to state whether abc is claimed. Said there is no argument that experts think works but needs checking.

events.time_since_posted: about 32 months; only blog commentary found
events.doubts: Mochizuki’s March 2024 report on Joshi’s series (filename ‘Report on a certain series of preprints (2024-03)’; the PDF was binary to my tools, so this rests on a search snippet) calls the series ‘mathematically meaningless’ and disputes the consultees. Woit’s January 2024 comments record expert doubt.
events.direction: Claims a step (Corollary 3.12) of the IUT argument. It cuts for that step, not for abc directly.

events.what_happened: Kirti Joshi, ‘Construction of Arithmetic Teichmüller Spaces IV: Proof of the abc-conjecture’ (arXiv 2403.10430, sole author, v1 15 March 2024). The abstract says the theory of Arithmetic Teichmüller Spaces, ‘using Shinichi Mochizuki’s rubric’, leads to a proof of the abc-conjecture. The v2 comments (24 February 2025) call it ‘an expanded and revised edition of my March 2024 submission and fixes the issues with the previous version’ (80 pages). The v2 HTML (read to about 100k of about 232k characters) describes itself as a ‘Preliminary version for comments’, carries ‘[This is still a work in progress!]’, and says ‘This paper completes (in Theorem 7.1.1) the remarkable proof of the abc-conjecture announced by Shinichi Mochizuki’. Scholze reportedly identified a mistake at Proposition 6.10.7 (nLab, citing a MathOverflow post by Scholze, ‘Global character of ABC/Szpiro inequalities’, version dated 2024-03-29; the MathOverflow post was not located or opened).
events.revisions: v2 24 February 2025 (per arXiv comments). Joshi’s FAQ on the proof appeared in November 2025 and was revised in May 2026 (per his site listing; not opened).
events.delivers: Claims a proof of the abc conjecture as stated, for all ε > 0. Its abstract names no hypothesis.
events.remains: Nothing in its own abstract. Joshi’s 2025 report frames the claim as conditional on acceptance of enhancements (see joshi-2025-final-report). Whether the theory built on Mochizuki’s rubric is established is the point in dispute.

checked_by.qualification: Arithmetic geometer; co-author of the 2018 critique of the IUT argument
checked_by.what_they_did: Reportedly identified a mistake in Joshi’s proof at Proposition 6.10.7, in a MathOverflow post (reported via nLab; not opened)

checked_by.qualification: Author of the IUT theory; a party to the dispute, so not independent
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a March 2024 report calling Joshi’s preprints ‘mathematically meaningless’ (search snippet only)

events.time_since_posted: about 31 months; no independent acceptance found
events.doubts: (a) Scholze’s reported error at Proposition 6.10.7 (via nLab; the MathOverflow thread was not read). (b) Mochizuki’s rejection; he is a party. (c) Framing shifts: the v2 HTML says the paper ‘completes’ Mochizuki’s proof; the 2025 Final Report is reported as concluding abc is proven only if the enhancements are accepted (Earth.com), and an AI referee calls that report’s conclusion not self-contained (Pith). (d) Woit (search summary of a 2025 post) reports experts unconvinced, and no one who has read it carefully in detail.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture as stated, so cuts for it.

events.what_happened: Tim Browning, Jared Duker Lichtman and Joni Teräväinen, ‘Bounds on the exceptional set in the abc conjecture’ (arXiv 2410.12234, v1 16 October 2024). Theorem 1.2 in v1: N_λ(X) = O(X^(33/50)) for fixed λ in (0, 1.001), where N_λ(X) counts coprime triples a + b = c with c ≤ X and rad(abc) < c^λ. The abstract describes a power-saving bound from density bounds on integer points, geometry of numbers and Fourier analysis. v1 acknowledgements mention funding only; the introduction says the exponent ‘can be reduced with substantial computer assistance’, which refers to computation, not AI.
events.revisions: v2 9 May 2026: author list now C. Bernert, T. Browning, J. D. Lichtman, J. Teräväinen (Bernert first). Theorem 1.2 becomes N_λ(X) ≪ X^((23λ+3)/40+ε) for λ in (0,2]; a new Theorem 1.3 gives X^(0.6+ε) for λ in (0,1). v2 cites Bernert’s arXiv 2506.13364 as [1] and thanks Bhavik Mehta for Lean help with ‘parts of an earlier version’. I did not check whether the 0.6 exponent appeared before v2.
events.delivers: v1: the count of exceptional triples with c ≤ X is at most X^(33/50+ε) for fixed λ in (0, 1.001). v2: X^(0.6+ε) for λ in (0,1) and X^((23λ+3)/40+ε) for λ in (0,2]. These are counts of the conjecture’s own exceptional set; they do not give finiteness.
events.remains: Finiteness of the exceptional set for each ε > 0. The bounds allow infinitely many exceptions, so the finiteness claim is untouched.

checked_by.qualification: Lean formalisation specialist; maintainer of the ABCExceptions Lean project
checked_by.what_they_did: Assisted with Lean verification of parts of an earlier version (acknowledgement only; the final statement is not stated to be checked)

events.doubts: None specific to the bound. The Lean project’s status is unclear: its page says both ‘we show’ and ‘ongoing’, and gives no sorry status. The exponents in v1 and v2 are different claims from the same source.
events.direction: Counting bound on the conjecture’s exceptional set. It cuts weakly for finiteness and does not decide it.
people: Christian Bernert (author of v2 first position)

events.what_happened: Kirti Joshi, ‘Final Report on the Mochizuki-Scholze-Stix Controversy’ (arXiv 2505.10568, single version, submitted 29 April 2025). The abstract (read) describes it as the author’s findings on the controversy and does not mention abc. Secondary reports say it (i) calls the Scholze–Stix assertions mathematically false (Table 2); (ii) says Mochizuki’s proof is incomplete because a Teichmüller theory of number fields is not established; and (iii) concludes that abc is proven provided Joshi’s enhancements are accepted (Earth.com, 13 June 2025, opened: he ‘boldly declares that the abc conjecture is indeed proven, provided his enhancements are accepted’). The PDF was binary and unreadable to my tools, so (i) to (iii) rest on secondary reports.
events.delivers: Per secondary reports only: abc proven, conditional on acceptance of Joshi’s enhancements (arithmetic holomorphic structures; an Arithmetic Teichmüller Datum). The abstract itself says only ‘findings’.
events.remains: Whether the enhancements are accepted, and whether the uniqueness of the theory built from Mochizuki’s Key Principle holds (the AI referee says it is unproved).

checked_by.who: Pith Review (AI referee, model named as deepseek-v4-flash)
checked_by.qualification: Automated referee; not a human reading
checked_by.what_they_did: Reviewed the paper on 16 August 2026. Editor’s note: REJECT, low confidence. Major objection: ‘A chain of citations to unrefereed arXiv preprints cannot, by itself, establish a proof of the abc conjecture.’ Also says the claim that every Scholze–Stix assertion is false is not engaged with their arguments, and that the uniqueness claim is unproved. It states that no human expert has reviewed the paper.

checked_by.qualification: IUT author; a party to the dispute
checked_by.what_they_did: Dismissed Joshi’s corrections as ‘profoundly misguided’ (per Earth.com)

events.time_since_posted: about 17 months; no human expert verification found
events.doubts: (a) The AI referee’s objections above: the conclusion depends on unrefereed preprints; the uniqueness claim is unproved; the blanket rejection of Scholze–Stix is not engaged. (b) The author is a party, and the press framing is conditional. (c) The July 2026 LANA report and Joshi’s own July 2026 comments on it disagree (see lana-2026-interim).
events.direction: Claims abc is proven, conditional per the secondary reports. Cuts for the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Brian Simpson, Zenodo record 15460771, ‘ABC’ (version v4 shown; publication date 18 May 2025), described as an ‘early Octomorphic mathematical reformulation/proof-attempt concerning the ABC Conjecture’. It is labelled ‘STATUS: HIGH_CLAIM_ARCHIVE’ and ‘CURRENT AUTHORITY: No’, and states ‘This record is not a current accepted proof of the ABC Conjecture’.
events.revisions: Only v4 was read. Earlier versions were not checked, so this date is the shown version’s, not necessarily the first.
events.delivers: A self-described proof attempt. The record’s own text says nothing is established.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: The author disclaims the record as current authority.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture; the claim is not established by the record.

events.what_happened: Jared Duker Lichtman (Stanford), ‘The abc conjecture is true almost always’ (arXiv 2505.13991, single version, 20 May 2025). An expository note using de Bruijn’s classical estimate: there are at most O(N^(2/3)) coprime triples (a, b, c) with a + b = c in {1, ..., N}^3 with rad(abc) < c^(1-ε) (abstract; Theorem 1.1 in the HTML). The HTML does not make the quantifier over ε explicit in the bound.
events.delivers: A counting bound: O(N^(2/3)) exceptional triples up to N. It bounds the count of the conjecture’s own exceptional set, but a bound that grows with N does not give finiteness.
events.remains: Finiteness of the exceptional set for each ε > 0.
events.direction: Power-saving count bound; cuts weakly for finiteness (exceptions are rare) and does not decide it.

events.what_happened: Christian Bernert (Leibniz Universität Hannover), ‘The exceptional set in the abc conjecture’ (arXiv 2506.13364, v1 16 June 2025, single version). Its abstract says it improves on and simplifies the work of Browning, Lichtman and Teräväinen, using two of their four methods. Theorem 1 (v1 HTML): N_λ(X) ≪ X^((23λ+3)/40+ε) for λ in (0,2). At λ = 1 the text gives X^(0.65+ε).
events.delivers: A count bound on the exceptional set: X^((23λ+3)/40+ε) for λ in (0,2), and X^(0.65+ε) at λ = 1.
events.remains: Finiteness of the exceptional set for each ε > 0.
events.direction: Counting bound; cuts weakly for finiteness and does not decide it.

events.what_happened: Runbo Li, ‘On the exceptional set in the abc conjecture’ (arXiv 2507.02885, v1 19 June 2025, single version). Theorem 1.3: the number of triples with c ≤ X is O(X^(56/85+ε)) for any ε > 0, for 0 < λ < 1 + δ(ε). The abstract calls this an improvement on O(X^(33/50)).
events.delivers: A count bound: X^(56/85+ε) (about X^(0.6588)) for λ near 1.
events.remains: Finiteness of the exceptional set for each ε > 0.
events.direction: Counting bound; cuts weakly for finiteness and does not decide it.

events.what_happened: Lemuel Schaine Harris, ‘Proof of the ABC Conjecture Finiteness via the Subspace Theorem and Explicit Height Bounds’ (Zenodo 16505191, v1, published 27 July 2025; file ABC_V11.pdf). The description says ‘Complete Proof of the ABC Conjecture Finiteness’. I read the metadata only, not the PDF. The subspace theorem is known to be related to abc but does not imply it (search summary citing Philippon, 1999).
events.delivers: Claimed complete proof of finiteness, per the description. The ε range is not stated in the metadata and the PDF was not read.
events.remains: Unknown without the PDF.
events.doubts: Zenodo does not peer-review. The description is the only content I read.
events.direction: Claims finiteness, so cuts for the conjecture if correct.

events.what_happened: MAEKI, HIDEMITSU, ‘Proof of the ABC Conjecture via Ghost Drift Theory’ (Zenodo 16746726, preprint v1.0, 5 August 2025, CC BY 4.0). The abstract (read in part) says it ‘presents an attempt to prove the ABC Conjecture’, recasts the finiteness assertion as equivalent to finite energy explosions in an author-defined ‘semantic space’ with a ‘Semantic Heart Point’, and claims ‘a clear geometric boundary’ identifies the exceptions. Files: GhostDrift_Semantic_ABC.pdf and AI_Reviews_on_ABC_Proof.pdf (468.5 kB). A Medium press release (search snippet: three AI models, GPT-4o, Gemini and Copilot, ‘confirmed’ the proof, with a later update about GPT-5) returned HTTP 403 and was not opened.
events.revisions: v1.0 shown; Zenodo says a newer version exists (not checked).
events.delivers: A claimed proof of finiteness within an author-defined framework. The record establishes nothing checkable.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: Self-published; the framework is author-defined; no independent expert or journal found. The AI ‘confirmations’ are checking claims, not expert verification (see ai).
events.direction: Claims the conjecture, so cuts for it if correct.

events.what_happened: Christopher Pompetzki, Zenodo record 18916301 (issued 8 March 2026, v1), a proof claim with a title ending ‘(Smirks)’. The abstract (read in part) says ‘We establish a certified chain of statements … toward the ABC Conjecture’, gets E ≤ 3 log c · log(log2 c), then E ≤ 2 log rad(abc) + K_ε by identifying v_p(abc) − 1 with a ‘spectral defect’ and applying a bound of Brock–Jordan–Poonen–Scholl–Wetherell, and concludes ‘The ABC Conjecture follows.’ The description includes informal text. I could not locate the cited Brock et al. bound in searches.
events.delivers: Claimed unconditional proof, per the abstract. The cited bound was not located.
events.remains: Nothing, by the claim.
events.doubts: Zenodo, no review. Informal text in the description. The cited bound could not be located. The PDF was not read.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture, so cuts for it if correct.

events.what_happened: ZEN Mathematics Center (ZEN University) announced Project LANA (‘Lean for ANAbelian geometry’) on 31 March 2026, an international project with Utrecht University and the University of Alberta. Its aims are to formalise anabelian geometry in Lean and to verify IUT theory with computer assistance. Fumiharu Kato is Project Leader (per a search summary of the ZMC announcement, which I did not open).
events.delivers: No mathematical result. A project to formalise IUT.
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: None: a project announcement.

events.what_happened: Ken Ono, Evan Chen (submitter), Kenny Lau and 21 others, ‘ABC implies that Ramanujan’s tau function misses almost all primes’ (arXiv 2603.29970; v1 31 March 2026, v2 8 April 2026, v3 25 April 2026, with the comment ‘Minor edits that address two referee reports’). Assuming abc, it bounds the number of primes ℓ ≤ X with |τ(n)| = ℓ for some n. The v1 HTML gives Theorem 1: S(X) = O(X^(9/10) log X). The v3 abstract (read) gives X^(13/22). The paper states: ‘AxiomProver autonomously proved and formalized Theorem 1 assuming Proposition 5.4 of [24].’ and ‘After AxiomProver generated a solution, the human authors wrote this paper (without the use of AI) for human readers.’
events.revisions: v2 8 April 2026; v3 25 April 2026 (minor edits addressing two referee reports; the journal is not named).
events.delivers: Conditional on abc: a bound on the prime values of τ, and a density-1 set of primes missed by τ. Nothing unconditional about abc.
events.remains: The abc conjecture itself, which the paper assumes.
events.doubts: The Theorem 1 exponent changes between v1 (9/10 with log) and v3 (13/22 in the abstract), and the reason is not given in what I read. The repository (github.com/AxiomMath/ramanujan-tau-misses-primes, per a search snippet) was not opened, so the sorry status is unverified.
events.direction: A conditional result on a neighbouring quantity. Cuts for abc only as a hypothesis.

systems.name: AxiomProver
systems.what_it_did: Autonomously produced and formalised in Lean/Mathlib the proof of Theorem 1, which is conditional on abc, from a natural-language statement. The authors say the human authors wrote the paper after the system generated the solution. This is load-bearing for the conditional theorem, not for abc.
systems.basis_quote: AxiomProver autonomously proved and formalized Theorem 1 assuming Proposition 5.4 of [24].

events.what_happened: Patrick Letendre, ‘The abc Conjecture Revisited’ (arXiv 2607.07641; v1 8 July 2026, v2 21 July 2026). It proposes a new abc-type conjecture and gives a main result about W(x,y), the sum of ω(x+j) for j = 1 to y, which holds under that new conjecture: for each fixed y, the limsup of W(x,y) log log x / log x equals 1. It does not claim the classical abc conjecture.
events.delivers: A conditional statement under a new conjecture. Nothing on the classical abc conjecture.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. This is a different question (an analogue).
events.direction: Neutral to the classical conjecture; it proposes a different one.

events.what_happened: Project LANA interim report, ‘Computer-Assisted Verification of IUT Theory’, released at a ZEN Mathematics Center press conference on 17 July 2026. The PDF is on nLab; it was binary to my tools, so I rely on the ZMC announcement (opened). The announcement says the project ‘continues to suspend judgment on whether a proof of the abc conjecture has been obtained through IUT theory’. It names as remaining issues: how Corollary 3.12 follows from Theorem 3.11 in the third IUT paper (unclear to many members); how two calculations of q-pilot log-volumes are ‘tautologically equivalent’; and how one of several algorithm outputs is identified with the data determined by the input. It reports no completed Lean verification of IUT. Kato’s X post (search snippet, not opened) says: ‘The way the argument from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 is written in the IUT papers is unformalizable. But since Mochizuki’s explanation of this point has …’ and that the team reserves final judgement. A Woit blog post (search summary, not opened) says the team located the gap where Scholze and Stix located theirs.
events.delivers: No verdict on abc. It localises unclear steps in the derivation of Corollary 3.12 and says formal verification is not yet done.
events.remains: The abc status (suspended); the Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 step; the q-pilot and algorithm-identification steps.

checked_by.who: Fumiharu Kato and the LANA project (ZEN University, Utrecht, Alberta)
checked_by.qualification: Project members; Kato is Project Leader; the group includes Lean and anabelian-geometry specialists
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote the interim report and withheld a verdict

checked_by.qualification: Arizona mathematician; a party to the dispute
checked_by.what_they_did: Published comments on the LANA report, dated 30 July 2026 in a search summary (PDF binary to my tools), disputing its conclusions

events.doubts: (a) The team withholds a verdict, so ‘unformalizable’ is not a finding of falsity. An 80aj blog post (opened) reports ‘Lean confirms’ the step cannot be formalised and a ‘potential logical gap’; that overstates the announcement. (b) Joshi (per the search summary) says the report missed that the proof needs the Arithmetic Teichmüller Datum of a fixed number field. (c) The report says Mochizuki’s explanation is changing, so the target is moving.
events.direction: Localises an unresolved, possibly unformalisable step at the Corollary 3.12 derivation, the same step Scholze and Stix named. No verdict.

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, ‘Note on the Exceptional Set in the ABC Conjecture’ (arXiv 2608.16764, math.GM; v1 17 August 2026, v2 24 August 2026, v3 19 September 2026). Theorem 1.1, as read in the arXiv HTML: for any small ε > 0 and large x, E(x) is nonempty and #E(x) → ∞, where E(x) is the set of coprime triples a + b = c with c in (x, x+h], h = o(x), and c > c_ε rad(abc)^(1+ε). The abstract says ‘an infinite set unconditionally for any ε<2/35’; §5 derives the contradiction for ε < 2/33. The paper says: ‘The exceptional triples are closely related to counterexamples of the abc conjecture.’ The method (per the HTML summary): a y-smooth integer c in a short interval (Corollary 3.1, from smooth-number results in short intervals), b = p^5 for a prime p > y, and a = |p^5 − c|, giving rad(abc) ≤ x^(33/35+o(1)), then the inequality for large x. Theorem 4.7 is labelled a ‘sketch of the lengthy proof’.
events.delivers: If correct: for each small fixed ε (ε < 2/35 per the abstract, ε < 2/33 per §5), infinitely many coprime triples with c > c_ε rad(abc)^(1+ε). That contradicts the abc conjecture for those ε. It claims nothing for ε ≥ 2/35.
events.remains: For ε ≥ 2/35 nothing is claimed. Every other part of the problem stands unaffected by this note.
events.doubts: (i) Single-author, unrefereed preprint; no expert engagement found. (ii) Internal inconsistency: the abstract says ε < 2/35 and §5 uses ε < 2/33. (iii) Theorem 4.7 is a ‘sketch of the lengthy proof’; Corollary 3.1 relies on cited smooth-number results, and the paper calls its proof unconditional though the HTML summary notes a nearby conditional remark. (iv) A search summary says the note’s references do not account for the 2025 to 2026 exponent improvements; I did not verify this. (v) The same author’s 2006 note argued heuristically against the conjecture (carella-2006-note). (vi) A search summary read the inequality as pointing the opposite way; I could not verify that from the HTML.
events.direction: Claims infinitely many exceptions for small ε, so it cuts against the conjecture if correct.
events.object: No explicit triple family is given in the parts I read. The argument is existential: a y-smooth c in a short interval (Corollary 3.1), with b = p^5 and a = |p^5 − c| (Section 5), and the inequality claimed for large x. Whether these triples satisfy c > c_ε rad^(1+ε) is the claim.

events.what_happened: R. Laniewski, ‘Radical defects, Wieferich primes, and the abc conjecture’ (arXiv 2609.00039, math.GM; v1 29 August 2026, single version). It defines a radical excess for coprime a + b = c and calls a triple ‘transgressive’ at ε when the excess is non-negative. For the Mersenne family (1, 2^m − 1, 2^m) it claims transgression at ε = 0 exactly when 2^m − 1 is not squarefree, on exponents of density 47/210. It gives a defect formula involving Wieferich primes. It states abc as open (‘such triples are finite in number’) and says a Mersenne counterexample family would need infinitely many Wieferich primes with exponential defect growth.
events.delivers: Results at ε = 0 for the Mersenne family, a defect identity, and a necessary condition for counterexamples. The abstract states no result at a fixed ε > 0.
events.remains: The abc conjecture for every ε > 0.
events.doubts: The ε = 0 results do not bear on abc as stated. I read the abstract only.
events.direction: Neutral in the abstract. Its ε = 0 results do not cut either way on the stated conjecture.

events.what_happened: GitHub repository wyx66624/ABCConjecture, described as ‘Using AI to prove the ABC conjecture and formalize the proof in Lean’. Its README (read) says the repository ‘does not contain an unconditional proof or disproof of the standard abc conjecture’ and that ‘Neither end goal has been reached’. It contains verified local theorems, conditional reductions and finite computations. The Lean package proves a conditional theorem, FourStageProgram.abc_conjecture, from a hypothesis for which ‘no intended source construction of FourStageProgram has been supplied’. The README says ‘This repository is a research program and audit trail, not an announcement that the abc conjecture has been solved.’ It lists ‘Author: ChatGPT’, names ChatGPT-generated files including the manuscript and checkpoint documents, and mentions ‘Agent review’, which it says is not external peer review. The status date is 8 September 2026; checkpoint folders run from 30 August 2026. The owner is the GitHub user wyx66624.
events.revisions: Status date 8 September 2026 per the README. Repository creation and commit history were not checked.
events.delivers: Conditional reductions and a Lean theorem conditional on an unsupplied hypothesis. By the README’s own statement, no unconditional result on abc.
events.remains: The abc conjecture in full.

checked_by.qualification: Not external; the README itself says so
checked_by.what_they_did: An internal agent review; the README says it is not external peer review

events.doubts: The repository calls itself a research program, and its conditional theorem has no supplied hypothesis. The sorry count is not stated, although the README says its policy forbids sorry in new global claims.
events.direction: A conditional framework. It does not cut either way on the unconditional question.

systems.name: ChatGPT
systems.what_it_did: Listed by the README as the repository’s author; the README says the manuscript and checkpoint documents are ChatGPT-generated. Its output includes the conditional mathematics and the Lean package. The README does not name a model version.

disputes.summary: Whether the IUT argument proves abc. Mochizuki (2012; PRIMS 2021) says yes; Scholze and Stix (2018) say the step from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 is a gap that cannot be repaired. The July 2026 LANA interim report finds the same step unclear and suspends judgement.

Joshi’s 2024 Construction IV and 2025 Final Report say the Scholze–Stix objections are false and that abc is proved, or proved once enhancements are accepted. Mochizuki calls Joshi’s corrections ‘profoundly misguided’ and his 2024 series ‘mathematically meaningless’ (March 2024 report, search snippet). Scholze is reported (via nLab) to have found a mistake at Proposition 6.10.7.

Joshi’s framing varies: the Construction IV v2 HTML says the paper ‘completes’ Mochizuki’s proof and is a work in progress, while the Final Report is reported as concluding abc is proven only if his enhancements are accepted. Read as an unconditional claim, the Construction IV abstract is a candidate in-window claimed resolution; read conditionally, it is not.

LANA’s July 2026 outcome. The ZMC announcement says the team suspends judgement on abc and that the Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 derivation is unclear. Kato’s X post (search snippet) calls the argument ‘unformalizable’ as written. An 80aj blog post says Lean ‘confirms’ the step cannot be formalised; that overstates the report. Joshi (30 July 2026, per a search summary) disputes LANA’s conclusions.

The exceptional-set exponent. The v1 (October 2024) Browning, Lichtman and Teräväinen result gives X^(33/50). Bernert’s June 2025 paper gives (23λ+3)/40. The v2 revision (May 2026, Bernert first author) adopts Bernert’s exponent, cites his paper as [1], and adds an X^(0.6+ε) bound for λ < 1. Who owns the improved exponent is an attribution question, and the record keeps both dated events.
AxiomProver tau paper: v1 Theorem 1 gives S(X) = O(X^(9/10) log X); the v3 abstract gives O(X^(13/22)). The sources I read do not explain the change.

Carella (August 2026) claims infinitely many exceptional triples for small ε, which contradicts the conjecture if correct. One search summary called the note ‘consistent with abc’; that reading contradicts the theorem as read in the arXiv HTML, and I did not adopt it.

summary: Searches (49 queries, listed below) and opened sources give this picture. The problem’s own Wikipedia article (opened) still says the conjecture is ‘regarded as unproven by the mainstream mathematical community’. Mochizuki’s 2012 IUT claim (PRIMS 2021) is contested by Scholze and Stix (2018), who place the gap at the step from Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12. In the window, Kirti Joshi posted Construction III (24 January 2024, two days before the frozen revision, about Corollary 3.12 only; the abstract does not claim abc) and Construction IV (15 March 2024, claiming the abc proof; its v2 HTML calls itself a work in progress and says the paper ‘completes’ Mochizuki’s proof). Joshi’s Final Report (29 April 2025) is reported in Earth.com as concluding abc is proven if his enhancements are accepted; the abstract does not mention abc; a Pith AI referee (deepseek-v4-flash, 16 August 2026) rejects it as not self-contained, and the PDF was unreadable to my tools. The LANA project (launched 31 March 2026; interim report 17 July 2026) withholds judgement on abc and says the Corollary 3.12 derivation is unclear to many members; no completed Lean verification of IUT is reported. The close call is whether Joshi IV is an in-window claimed resolution. It is an author’s own arXiv claim, unrefereed and disputed, and I record it without deciding. Other in-window results are count bounds on the exceptional set (Browning–Lichtman–Teräväinen 2024 and its May 2026 revision; Lichtman, May 2025; Bernert, June 2025; Li, June 2025). These move a count the conjecture names, but a count that grows with N or X does not give finiteness, so I record them as moving the count and not settling finiteness. The Carella note (17 August 2026, revised to 19 September) claims #E(x) → ∞ for small ε (ε < 2/35 in the abstract, ε < 2/33 in §5). If correct it contradicts the conjecture for those ε; it is unrefereed, shows no expert engagement, has the internal ε mismatch, and calls its Theorem 4.7 proof a sketch. Several fringe Zenodo claims (Ben Hadj Salem 2019, Simpson 2025, Harris 2025, Ghost Drift 2025, Pompetzki 2026) claim proofs with no review; I read only metadata or abstracts for most. On AI: the only system credited with load-bearing mathematics in the window is AxiomProver, in a conditional result on the Ramanujan tau function, with the authors’ own quoted account. The only other AI-authored item is a GitHub repository listing ‘Author: ChatGPT’, whose README says it is conditional and not an abc proof. The Ghost Drift AI ‘confirmations’ (press release, not opened) and the Pith AI referee are checking roles only. No source credits an AI system with the abc resolution, and the AI-discovery searches found no abc result (OpenAI’s ten August 2026 results, the October 2026 OpenAI manuscript release, the Erdős trackers and Gil Kalai’s October 2026 post contain no abc result).
competing_reading: Joshi IV can be read as an in-window claimed resolution: an arithmetic geometer posted an arXiv paper in March 2024 claiming the abc proof outright, and its v2 says it ‘completes’ the proof. On that reading the problem moved in the window, though the claim is unrefereed and disputed. Against this, the LANA team, the 2018 critics, and the Wikipedia lead all treat the status as unresolved, and the 2025 report frames the same claim as conditional. Separately, Carella’s note could be read as a genuine infinite-exception result, if its ε range and Theorem 4.7 hold. That would contradict a conjecture most experts believe, so I treat it as very unlikely but unrefereed.
what_would_settle_it: For the IUT line: a referee report or journal decision on Joshi IV and the Final Report from a number theorist outside the dispute; a completed Lean formalisation of Theorem 3.11 to Corollary 3.12 (the LANA project), or a Mochizuki reply addressing the points in the July 2026 interim report; Scholze’s MathOverflow thread on Proposition 6.10.7. For Carella: an expert reading of §3 to §5, a check of the ε range (2/35 versus 2/33) and of Theorem 4.7. For the exceptional-set line: which exponent the published (v2) version settles on, and whether any argument for finiteness exists (none seen). For AxiomProver: the reason the Theorem 1 exponent changed between v1 and v3.
